script: The dog with a statue in Central Park wasn't even the one who did the hardest part of the run. January 1925, Nome, Alaska. Diphtheria was spreading, and children were dying. The only serum was six hundred seventy-four miles away. Twenty mushers and over a hundred fifty dogs relayed it across Alaska in a blizzard, temperatures near forty below. Leonhard Seppala and his lead dog Togo, twelve years old, ran the longest and most dangerous leg: two hundred sixty-four miles, including a shortcut across frozen sea ice in a whiteout. The final fifty-five miles went to a musher named Gunnar Kaasen and his dog, Balto. Balto's team reached Nome first. He got the headlines, a movie, and a statue in Central Park. metadata.title: Random But True: The Sled Dog Who Did The Hard Part And Got No Statue
metadata.caption:
January 1925, Nome, Alaska. A diphtheria outbreak threatened the town, and the only antitoxin serum was 674 miles away.

A relay of 20 mushers and over 150 sled dogs carried it across Alaska through a blizzard, temperatures near -40°F.

Leonhard Seppala and his lead dog Togo - 12 years old, near retirement age for a sled dog - ran the longest and most dangerous leg: 264 miles round trip, including a shortcut across the frozen, unstable ice of Norton Sound in a total whiteout. Other teams in the relay averaged about 31 miles each.

The final 55 miles into Nome went to musher Gunnar Kaasen and his dog, Balto. Balto's team arrived first - and got the headlines, a movie, and a statue in New York's Central Park that still stands today.

Togo covered nearly five times the distance, through the worst of the storm. Most dog-sledding historians and experts now agree his leg was the real defining moment of the run.
